standard.title: Media languages across contexts
standard.description: explore ways that media languages and media technologies are used in media arts works and practices across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can compare media arts works made for different purposes and explain how context shapes representations. They have not yet explored how media languages and technologies construct power relationships, stereotyping and bias — or systematically compared media representations across historical and cultural contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore how media languages and media technologies are used to construct representations across cultures, times, places and contexts — including analysis of stereotyping, power, bias and cultural values.

nodes.label: Representations and power
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how media language choices (framing, colour, costume) construct power relationships and status in representations of characters.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how framing, colour or costume is used in one media work to establish a character as high or low status — explaining the specific language choices that create that power relationship.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how status and power relationships are constructed through framing, colour, costume and setting (hero/villain creation); investigate stereotyping and bias in game characters and media representations; apply Viewpoints questions to analyse power: 'How can I use framing to demonstrate a power relationship between characters?'
wider: Investigate how status and power relationships are constructed through framing, colour and costume in a specific media form (e.g. advertising, game design, TV) — applying findings to original character design that deliberately constructs or challenges a power relationship

Compare how the same type of character (hero, villain, authority figure) is constructed differently in media works from different cultural contexts — identifying what the differences reveal about cultural values and assumptions
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how media languages construct power and status is the conceptual foundation for media literacy at Y5-6 — without it, students cannot critically analyse stereotyping, bias or ideological positioning in media.

response_modes.reason: Students need explicit scaffolding to move from 'this character looks powerful' to 'the low-angle shot and dark costume construct power because...' Use Viewpoints questions as an analytical framework.

success_criteria: Student can identify at least two media language choices (framing, colour, costume, setting) that construct a character's status or power
Student can explain how each choice communicates that status to the audience

nodes.label: Context, values and comparison
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare media representations created in different times, places and cultural contexts — explaining how context influences the values, characters and stories portrayed.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two media arts works representing the same topic (e.g. family, youth, heroes) from different times or cultural contexts — identifying at least two differences and explaining how context influenced each.
nodes.typical_width: Research and compare media representations from different times and places (e.g. family in TV across decades, safety campaigns across cultural contexts); explain how context influences values; investigate how media arts works share cultural information about communities; discuss the role of media arts in cultural knowledge sharing.
wider: Research and compare representations of a topic (e.g. family, youth, heroes) across multiple historical periods or cultural contexts — explaining what forces (social, economic, political) shaped each representation, and evaluating how audiences might have responded differently

Investigate how media arts works from different cultural contexts share information about people's relationships with their environment and community — comparing two culturally distinct examples and discussing what values are communicated

response_modes.reason: Vary the comparison contexts — different decades, different countries, different cultural contexts — so students develop genuine analytical range rather than a single comparison that may reinforce existing assumptions.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of contextual comparison available at Y5-6 (family across TV decades, cultural identity in advertising, First Nations identity in popular culture) is genuinely rich for critical media analysis.
success_criteria: Student can compare two media representations of the same topic from different contexts
Student can explain how context influenced at least two differences between the representations
